title: Root Canals and Pregnancy: Is It Safe to Wait?
metaTitle: Root Canals and Pregnancy: Is It Safe to Wait?
metaDescription: Is it safe to have a root canal while pregnant? Treating infection is often safer than waiting. Learn timing, X-ray and anaesthetic basics, and who to ask.
secondaryKeywords: is a root canal safe when pregnant
excerpt: Necessary dental care, including a root canal for an infected tooth, can often be done during pregnancy. Here is what to consider and who to involve.
heroImageAlt: Pregnant patient talking with a dentist about treatment options during pregnancy.
bodyHtml:
In general, necessary dental care — including a root canal to treat an infected tooth — can often be carried out during pregnancy, and treating an active infection is frequently considered safer than leaving it untreated. That said, timing and individual circumstances matter, and decisions should always be made with your dentist and, where appropriate, your physician or obstetrician. There is no one-size-fits-all answer, and no treatment can be described as risk-free, so this is a conversation to have with your care providers rather than a decision to make alone.

Why leaving an infection untreated carries its own risks

An infected tooth does not resolve on its own, and the stress, pain, and infection associated with an untreated dental problem are themselves worth avoiding during pregnancy. For this reason, guidance from dental and health organisations generally supports addressing dental infections and urgent problems during pregnancy rather than postponing care that is genuinely needed. Weighing the risk of treatment against the risk of leaving an infection is part of what your dentist will discuss with you.

Timing considerations

When treatment is elective and can wait, the second trimester is often described as a comfortable window for dental care, as the early weeks involve important early development and the later weeks can make lying back in the chair less comfortable. However, urgent problems — such as significant infection, swelling, or severe pain — may need to be dealt with when they arise rather than deferred. Your dentist will balance the urgency of the dental issue against where you are in your pregnancy, and there is no fixed rule that applies to everyone. It also helps to keep up with routine checkups during pregnancy, since hormonal changes can affect the gums, and catching problems early tends to make them simpler to manage.

Telling your dental team you are pregnant

Always let your dentist know you are pregnant, how far along you are, and about any complications or advice from your physician. This information shapes decisions about:

  • X-rays. Dental X-rays use very low doses and are taken with protective measures, but during pregnancy dentists limit them to what is necessary and discuss timing with you.
  • Local anaesthetic and medications. Your dentist will choose approaches appropriate for pregnancy and coordinate with your physician where needed, including for any pain relief or antibiotics.
  • Positioning and comfort. Small adjustments can make treatment more comfortable, especially later in pregnancy.

Working with both your dentist and physician

For anything beyond routine care, it is sensible for your dentist and your physician or obstetrician to be on the same page. If you have a higher-risk pregnancy or specific medical considerations, your physician's input helps ensure the plan is right for you. This shared approach, rather than any blanket rule, is what makes care during pregnancy appropriate for your individual situation. You can learn more about what treatment involves on the root canal therapy at Smile Dental Arts Centre page.

Is it safe to wait until after the baby is born?

It depends on the problem. A painful infection usually should not wait, because leaving it carries its own risks. Truly elective work can sometimes be scheduled for a more comfortable time. Your dentist will help you decide.

Are dental X-rays safe during pregnancy?

Dental X-rays use very low doses and protective shielding, and are generally considered low-risk, but during pregnancy they are kept to what is necessary. Tell your dentist you are pregnant so they can take appropriate precautions.

Can I have anaesthetic for a root canal while pregnant?

Local anaesthetic is commonly used in dental care during pregnancy, with choices tailored to your situation. Discuss any concerns with your dentist and physician.

Getting advice for your situation

If you are pregnant and have a tooth that may need a root canal, the best step is a conversation with your dentist, in coordination with your physician, about what is appropriate and when. Dr. Neda Kadivar, a general and family dentist with over 20 years of experience, can discuss your options with you at the team at Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham, Ontario.

This article is general information and not a substitute for professional dental advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always speak with a licensed dentist about your specific situation.
